AI Impact on the Global Job Market

Risk, Salary & Skills Trend Analysis (2015–2035)

Executive Overview

This report examines the evolving relationship between Artificial Intelligence, global job markets, skills, and salaries from 2015 through 2035. By analyzing over 12,000 synthetic records simulating realistic global trends, we uncover critical insights for strategic workforce planning.

Key Takeaways

  • Rising Automation Risk: The average AI risk score has surged from 0.30 in 2015 to a projected 0.51 by 2035, highlighting an urgent need for adaptive reskilling across vulnerable sectors.
  • Salary & Risk Correlation: There is a negative correlation (-0.24) between salary and AI risk, indicating that lower-paying roles tend to face higher automation threats, while premium salaries are shielded by advanced technical skills.
  • Divergent Job Survival: While roles like AI Researcher and Cybersecurity Analyst maintain near 100% survival rates, Business Analysts face a starkly lower survival prospect of just 43.0%.

AI Automation Risk Landscape

The distribution of AI automation risk varies significantly by role and geography. Some roles exhibit steeper increases in risk over time as AI capabilities expand.

Key Finding: The Business Analyst role experiences the highest average automation risk, whereas AI Researcher remains the most secure across the measured timeline.

Salary Trends & Segmentation

Compensation trends reveal the premium placed on experience and specific skills. Notably, there is a complex correlation between salary levels and AI risk: highly compensated senior roles may face distinct types of AI augmentation or risk compared to entry-level positions.

Insight: The negative correlation (-0.24) between Salary and AI Risk illustrates that higher salaries generally correspond to more secure, technically complex roles. However, experience level acts as a strong modifier—Senior positions command higher salaries while maintaining varying degrees of risk.

Skills Demand & Future-Proofing

Tracking skill demand scores over time identifies which competencies are gaining market relevance and which are depreciating.

Insight: Skills like Python and Java continue to dominate demand scores into 2035, while foundational skills face increased volatility as AI automation reshapes technical requirements.

Job Survival & Market Outlook

Job survival prospects (roles with a survival class of 1 or 2) and total job openings provide a clear picture of expanding versus contracting labor demand.

Insight: The stark contrast in survival rates—with Business Analysts dropping below 53% survival probability—demands immediate intervention in workforce planning.

Strategic Recommendations

  • Implement Continuous Reskilling for At-Risk Roles: With AI risk scores climbing to 0.51 by 2035, and roles like Business Analyst facing high vulnerability, organizations must invest in continuous learning programs transitioning employees toward low-risk domains.
  • Realign Compensation Strategies: As the salary premium for future-proof skills grows (demonstrated by the negative correlation between risk and pay), HR should pivot from traditional role-based banding to dynamic, skill-based compensation models prioritizing durable competencies like Python and Advanced Cloud Architecture.
  • Proactive Workforce Transitioning: For roles showing declining survival rates (e.g., Business Analyst) and contracting job openings toward 2035, initiate early transition pathways to move at-risk talent into adjacent, higher-survival categories (e.g., Data Science, AI Research).
  • Focus on Augmentation, Not Just Replacement: Equip mid-to-senior professionals in moderately at-risk categories with AI tools to augment their capabilities, shifting their value from routine task execution to strategic oversight and complex problem-solving.
